5. The spoken form: "Se lo sapevo, venivo"
In everyday speech, many Italians use the imperfetto in both parts for the impossible hypothesis:
Se partivi prima, arrivavi in tempo.
Se fossi partito prima, saresti arrivato in tempo.
You'll hear it often, especially in Naples or in films. Recognise it, but in exams and in writing use the correct form.

The news appeared in the papers three days later, even though Bellini had asked everyone not to say anything. "Hidden face discovered in the Syracuse Caravaggio," wrote the Corriere. The next day there were two TV crews in front of the church, six journalists and a queue of tourists stretching all the way to the sea. The sacristan, Signor Turi, a small bald man of seventy-five, had never seen so many people, not even at Easter.

"If I'd known, I'd have opened a bar," he told Matei, bringing him his coffee on the scaffolding as he did every morning. Turi had been the sacristan for fifty years and knew the painting better than anyone: he had dusted it, lit it, defended it from pigeons and thieves. "Fifty years I've been looking at it," he kept saying, shaking his head, "and I'd never seen that child. If you'd told me sooner, I'd have lit a candle for him."

The face was small, barely bigger than a hand, at the top right, in the great dark void above the figures. It was a child of five or six, with curly hair and wide-open eyes, looking at the saint lying on the ground. Caravaggio had painted him with a few quick strokes, as he always did, and then, for some reason, had covered him with a layer of black.

Why? That was the question everyone was asking. The journalists had a thousand theories. One wrote that if Caravaggio hadn't had to flee Malta, he would have finished the child. Another claimed the boy was the son of a Syracusan nobleman who had refused to pay. A third, more romantic, said Caravaggio had covered a portrait of himself as a child, because it was too painful.

Bellini didn't believe any of these theories. "If we had a letter from Caravaggio, we could know," he said. "But we don't. And in my opinion it's better that way. A mystery solved is a dead mystery." Then he would look at the little face for minutes on end, with his hands behind his back, and Giulia knew he was thinking of another child, the one in the 1966 photograph, in his grandfather's arms.

Viola came to church every day too. Giulia carried her in the baby carrier until eleven, then left her with Turi, who, having brought up six grandchildren, could rock her better than anyone. The old sacristan walked her among the columns and told her stories of saints in Sicilian. "If I'd been born fifty years later," he would tell her, "I'd have become a restorer too. But in my day there were no schools for that sort of thing. There were only brooms."

One evening, at dinner on Concetta's terrace, Matei and Giulia began a game that would last for weeks: the "what if" game. "If we hadn't met at the Uffizi," Giulia began, "you'd have gone back to Sibiu after a year." "And you'd have married a Neapolitan with a Vespa," Matei replied. "If we hadn't sent that report to Bellini, the painting wouldn't have been restored." "And if I hadn't got pregnant, we'd have restored it in February, without the new machine."

"And the child would have stayed in the dark," Matei concluded. They both looked towards the bedroom, where Viola was asleep in the travel cot, one arm raised above her head, as if she were waving to someone. Concetta, who was bringing the dessert, heard the last sentence. "You two think too much," she said. "If my husband had thought so much, he'd never have asked me to marry him. And now I'd be an old spinster in Palermo."

The real problem, though, was another one: what to do with the child? The Heritage Authority wanted to remove the black layer completely, to show the face to everyone. "It would be the discovery of the century," said the superintendent, a young and ambitious man. "If we leave it covered, nobody will ever see it." Bellini didn't agree. Matei and Giulia didn't know what to think.

In the end it was Turi, the sacristan, who settled the question, without realising it. One morning, bringing the coffee, he stopped in front of the painting and said, almost to himself: "If Caravaggio had wanted it to be seen, he wouldn't have covered it. He was a difficult man, but he knew what he was doing. If I were you, I'd let him sleep." Then he climbed slowly down the ladder and began sweeping the church as if he hadn't said anything.

That evening Bellini wrote a six-page letter to the superintendent. Matei and Giulia signed it with him. They proposed leaving the child under the black, as the painter had wanted, but showing visitors the X-ray next to the painting, on an illuminated panel. "That way anyone who wants to see him can," Giulia explained, "and Caravaggio stays Caravaggio."

The superintendent agreed after two weeks, almost reluctantly. If he had said no, Bellini would probably have chained himself to the scaffolding, and everyone knew it. When Matei gave Turi the news, the old sacristan said nothing. He just took a small white candle out of his pocket, lit it and placed it on the altar, right below the spot where the child was sleeping.

"I'd promised him," he said. "If you'd told me sooner, I'd have lit it sooner. But better late than never." And that evening, for the first time in fifty years, Turi locked the church without switching off all the lights.
